thread: Freedom that arrives too late: the person released is already the shape of what held them
summary: Each piece asks what is left to free once the long confinement has done its work. James argues it as a plain observation: habit fixes the person, and a discharged soldier, an old prisoner and a tiger with an open cage all return to what they know. Byron images it in a monologue where the captive has grown so close to his chains, his walls and the spiders that he leaves with a sigh and not a shout. Bierce dramatises it in the most literal way he can: a man gets his freedom, his flight, his home, and the story only lets him have it inside the moment where it cannot be used. Eagles sing around it: a place that is easy to enter, easy to enjoy and impossible to leave, with the door as the only thing that never moves.

pieces.essay: James argues it: habit is a flywheel that holds people where their earlier life put them, and he treats this as more mercy than prison.
pieces.poem: Byron images it: the prisoner's affection for his cell is the last chain, and it is the one that stays on after the others are struck off.
pieces.story: Bierce dramatises it: the escape is perfect in every detail, and the only reader who cannot see the cost is the man who is escaping.
pieces.song: Eagles sing around it: the narrator is a guest in a house that asks nothing of him except that he stays, and the song cannot end without the same refusal.

forYou: For When Jasmine Blooms: a society released into independence in 1957 has to walk out of institutions the colonisers designed, and a character who survives the era may find that the habits of being watched are the harder thing to give up.
